The time has come, spring is arriving with more and more force. Passionate barbecuers have been champing at the bit. Of course, classic bratwursts and collar steaks are the first thing to go on the grill.
Rost.et:
From Middle High German rōst, from Old High German rōst, from Proto-West Germanic *raust. Cognate with Middle Dutch rôost, Old Saxon rōst. From the related West Germanic verb *raustijan stems Old French rostir (“to roast”), whence English roast.

s: ... Dort seh’ ich Grane, mein selig Roß: \ wie weidet er munter der mit mir schlief! \ Mit mir hat ihn Siegfried erweckt. — Richard Wagner, Siegfried, Dritter Aufzug, Dritte Szene.
I see Grane there, my trusty steed: \ how happily he grazes, he who was asleep like me! \ Siegfried woke him along with me.

1914, His Majesty the Emperor of Germany Wilhelm II, An das Deutsche Volk
Wir werden uns wehren bis zum letzten Hauch von Mann und Roß
We shall defend ourselves to the last breath of man and horse
Ross.et: From Middle High German ros (“horse”), from Old High German ros, hros (“horse”), from Proto-West Germanic *hross.

Roß.et: From Middle High German rāz(e), from Old High German rāza, from Proto-West Germanic *hrātu. Roß was the Central German form, Wabe the Upper German; the latter was standardized around 1800.

Rostock.et: From Middle Low German Rozstoc, from a West Slavic language (probably Polabian), from Proto-Slavic *orz-tokъ (“river fork”). Compare Czech roztok.

Roswitha.et: From the Germanic elements Proto-Germanic *hrōþiz (“fame”) and *swinþaz (“strong”), via Old Saxon as evidenced by the loss of -n-.

rosig.et: Inherited from Middle High German rōsic. By surface analysis, Rose + -ig.

rostig.et: From Middle High German rostec, from Old High German rostag, from Proto-Germanic *rustagaz (“rusty”), equivalent to Rost (“rust”) + -ig (“-y”). Cognate with English rusty.

In extreme cases, in their love for their parents children can even learn to be obsequious comrades-in-arms in the “War of the Roses”, mutating into the executioner of their own vital interests.
2013, Jürgen Wirth, Manisch-Depressiv – Ein Mann sieht rot, edition winterwork, Kapitel 15, Tag 11

What agony I had to go through during the eight months of our “War of the Roses”, when my wife continued to attack me, constantly informed me I had no rights except for paying, constantly made sure that the children did not come into contact with me, and used the house to pressure me financially.
Rosenkrieg.et: From Der Rosenkrieg, the German name of the 1989 American film The War of the Roses, a pun on etymology 1 above.
